title: TESS and Kepler transit depths of Kepler-1658 b differ by 9 +- 5 percent, less than the 29 percent that the proposed bound K-dwarf eclipsing binary predicts (24 control planets)
abstract: Question: Winn & Stefansson (2025) said that Kepler-1658 b (KOI-4.01) is not a planet but a bound eclipsing binary, in which a K dwarf that gives 1.73 percent of the Kepler-band light is eclipsed by an M dwarf. A K dwarf is redder than the F-type primary, so this model predicts a deeper eclipse in the TESS band than in the Kepler band. A planet gives the same radius ratio in both bands. Method: We fitted 15 Kepler long-cadence quarters (2009-2013, 250 transits) and all 7 TESS 2-minute sectors (2021-2024, 42 transits) with one planet model: geometry from Kepler, PHOENIX limb darkening for each band, and a bootstrap over transits. The same code measured 24 confirmed Kepler giant planets as controls. We predicted the binary-model ratio with PHOENIX spectra, the two band responses and injected eclipses. Results: The TESS/Kepler depth ratio of Kepler-1658 b is 1.094 +- 0.038. The controls give a mean of 1.004 +- 0.008 with a scatter of 0.023, so the calibrated ratio is 1.089 +- 0.045. A main-sequence K dwarf (4720 K, 0.72 R_sun) that gives the fitted dilution predicts 1.29 (range 1.27-1.32), which is 4.5 sigma above the data. A planet (1.00) is 2.0 sigma below the data. The 7 TESS sectors agree with each other, 13 crowding-matched controls give the same calibration, and detrending variants give 1.06-1.15. Conclusion: The TESS data do not show the colour signal of the proposed bound K-dwarf eclipsing binary. Only an eclipsed star with nearly the colour of the primary (5400 K or hotter) agrees with the data, and a bound main-sequence star of that temperature is too luminous for the fitted dilution. Limitations: The test depends on the pipeline crowding corrections (10 percent for Kepler-1658 in TESS) and on PHOENIX limb darkening at impact parameter 0.92. If the Kepler limb darkening is free and the TESS limb darkening is fixed (an inconsistent combination that the Kepler data do not prefer), the controls scatter by 9 percent and Kepler-1658 gives 1.24 +- 0.11, which does not separate the two models. The result does not explain the velocity and cross-correlation anomalies that Winn & Stefansson reported, and it does not exclude a blend with a star of the same colour. display.caption: TESS/Kepler transit-depth ratio (k_TESS/k_Kepler)^2 of Kepler-1658 b (red) and 24 control Kepler giant planets (grey), all fitted with the same code. Grey band: control mean +- scatter. Blue line and band: bound-binary predictions for an eclipsed star of 4720 K (main sequence) to 5400 K.

Phase-folded, binned Kepler (left) and TESS (right) transits of Kepler-1658 b with the planet-model fit (red). Dashed blue: the TESS transit that the main-sequence bound-binary model predicts. Visible depths differ also because of the 29.4-min Kepler exposures and the weaker TESS limb darkening; the fit includes both.

Predicted TESS/Kepler depth ratio of the bound-binary model against the temperature of the eclipsed star B (flux-ratio term, and full injection-fit prediction), with the control-calibrated Kepler-1658 measurement (red band) and the planet value (black).
